strengths: Presents a well-motivated, unifying probabilistic framework (Product of Experts) that generalizes composition of heterogeneous generative and discriminative models (diffusion/flow models, autoregressive models, VLMs, physics simulators) at inference time, without retraining.

Provides a concrete and practical sampling algorithm (AIS + SMC with conditional generative expert composition) with clear derivations connecting flow-model score functions to the annealed sampling procedure.

Demonstrates broad applicability across diverse tasks: graphics-engine-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, and regionally composed text-to-image generation, showing the framework's flexibility for different input modalities (text, image, low-level pose/trajectory).
Includes an alternative autoregressive instantiation (Appendix C) showing the framework generalizes beyond flow-based diffusion models.
Provides ablation studies (e.g., conditional sampling, particle counts) that support specific design choices in the framework.
Combines both automatic quantitative metrics (LPIPS, MSE, VBench-style scores) and VLM-based (GPT-4o) evaluation across multiple perceptual dimensions (controllability, quality, alignment).
The intermediate sample visualizations (Fig. 8) offer useful insight into how the SMC resampling process improves alignment over iterations.
weaknesses: Evaluation datasets are quite small (e.g., 30 scenes for image editing, 12 scenes for physics-instructed video generation), limiting the statistical robustness of the reported metrics and their standard deviations.

Most experiments compose only 2 generative/discriminative experts, which is a fairly limited demonstration of the claimed generality of combining many heterogeneous knowledge sources; scalability to larger numbers of experts is not empirically shown.

Baselines are relatively narrow (single baseline per task: RF-Solver, monolithic Wan2.1 variants, PhysGen3D), and the paper does not compare against other SMC-based or compositional reward-steering methods cited in related work (e.g., [46, 55]), making it harder to assess relative advantages.

The key approximation used for annealed discriminative rewards (r_t(x) ≈ r(x̂)) and the conditional sampling update (Eq. 7) rely on heuristic justifications rather than rigorous theoretical analysis of bias or convergence guarantees.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o as an evaluation judge for multiple metrics raises reproducibility and potential bias concerns; no human evaluation is included despite central claims about improved 'user controllability.'
Computational overhead is substantial (up to ~30 minutes per video sample) but not directly benchmarked against baseline inference costs in terms of quality-per-compute tradeoffs.
Quantitative improvements in some settings (e.g., Table 2, physics-instructed video generation) are modest or mixed across metrics, weakening the strength of the controllability claims.
Limited discussion/empirical exploration of failure cases where experts are incompatible, despite this being noted as a core assumption/limitation of the method.

strengths: Proposes a unified probabilistic framework (Product of Experts) that combines heterogeneous knowledge sources — visual generative models, discriminative VLM rewards, and non-neural physics simulators — for visual generation, going beyond prior compositional generation work that mostly focuses on homogeneous generative experts.

Provides a concrete, practical implementation (Algorithm 1) combining Annealed Importance Sampling with Sequential Monte Carlo, including detailed constructions for both flow-based and autoregressive generative experts (main text and Appendix C).

Demonstrates the framework across a genuinely diverse set of applications: graphics-engine-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, and regional text-to-image composition with VLM discriminative guidance.
Includes ablations that isolate the contribution of key design choices, e.g., the conditional-sampling scheme (Eq. 7) and particle count in SMC, which show measurable degradation when removed.

Compares against reasonably relevant baselines (RF-Solver, PhysGen3D, Depth2V/Image2V/Traj2V) and provides both quantitative metrics and qualitative visualizations (including intermediate particle visualizations in Appendix E.2) that help illustrate how the method behaves.
weaknesses: Evaluation is conducted on very small, custom-built datasets (e.g., 30 scenes for image object insertion, 12 scenes for physics-instructed video, 9 scenes from PhysGen3D), which limits confidence in the generality and statistical robustness of the reported improvements; several reported metric differences are smaller than their standard deviations.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o as an automatic evaluator for controllability, quality, and alignment scores raises concerns about evaluation validity and potential bias, with no human study to corroborate these judgments.

The method is computationally expensive (up to ~30 minutes per video sample per Appendix B), which is a substantial practical limitation not thoroughly analyzed in terms of scaling behavior as the number of experts grows — the paper explicitly defers 'large-scale PoE sampling' to future work, leaving the framework's scalability an open question.

Several core approximations are introduced without rigorous theoretical justification: the single-step Euler flow-ODE composition used as an MCMC initializer, and the Gaussian approximation used to derive the conditional-expert update (Eq. 7) rely on heuristic arguments (Appendix D.2) rather than formal guarantees of correctness or convergence.

The technical machinery (AIS, SMC-based reward steering, PoE formulation) is largely adapted from existing prior work (Neal 2001; Hinton 2002; Wu et al. 2023; Zhao et al. 2024), so the primary contribution is the application/engineering integration into the visual generation domain rather than a fundamentally new sampling or compositional algorithm.

Baseline comparisons are sometimes not fully matched in input information (e.g., RF-Solver only receives a coarse text prompt while the proposed method receives precise graphics-engine pose specifications), which may inflate the apparent controllability gap rather than isolating the benefit of the PoE composition itself.

The text-to-image regional composition experiments (Section 4.4) lack standard, widely-used quantitative benchmarks (e.g., FID, CLIPScore, or comparisons to established regional-composition baselines like MultiDiffusion/DiffCollage), relying instead on a small set of qualitative examples and VQAScore-based numbers embedded mostly in figures rather than a comprehensive table.

The number of jointly composed experts demonstrated in each application is small (typically 2 generative + at most 1 discriminative), so the claimed benefit of flexibly composing many heterogeneous experts is not empirically stress-tested at a scale that would strongly support the paper's motivating claims.

strengths: Presents a unifying probabilistic Product-of-Experts framework that can combine heterogeneous sources (diffusion/flow generative models, autoregressive models, VLM-based discriminative rewards, and physics-simulator-derived signals) at inference time without retraining, which is a conceptually appealing and practically useful contribution.

Technically sound sampling procedure combining Annealed Importance Sampling with per-timestep MCMC kernels and SMC-style resampling, explicitly contrasted with path-wise importance weighting used in concurrent work (Skreta et al. 2025, He et al. 2025) to avoid weight degeneracy.

Demonstrates the framework's versatility across three distinct and practically motivated applications: graphics-engine-instructed image object/character insertion, physics-simulator-instructed video generation (both flow-based and autoregressive), and layout-controlled text-to-image generation.

Reasonably thorough empirical comparisons against multiple relevant, recent, strong baselines (RF-Solver, Magic Insert, Add-it, FLUX-Fill, SDEdit, PhysGen3D, 3DIS-FLUX) using a mix of automated metrics (MSE, LPIPS, IoU, VQAScore) and GPT-4o-based evaluation.

Useful ablations isolating the effect of conditional sampling (Eq. 6) and particle count/SMC resampling, and a clear specification of practical instantiations for flow and autoregressive experts (Section 3.3, Appendix C).
weaknesses: Evaluation datasets are quite small in most tasks (e.g., 30, 80, 12, 9, and 50 scenes), limiting statistical robustness of the reported improvements and raising concerns about generalization to larger-scale or more diverse settings.

No human/user study is conducted to validate controllability or perceptual quality claims; the paper relies heavily on GPT-4o as an automatic judge, which can introduce its own biases and is not independently validated for this specific evaluation protocol.

Ablation results are mixed: Table 4 shows that removing SMC resampling sometimes yields comparable or even better mIoU, partially undercutting the claimed benefit of SMC, and the paper does not fully reconcile this tension.

The framework is only demonstrated with a small number of experts (2-3) per task; the paper's motivating claim of integrating "many heterogeneous" experts is not stress-tested at larger scale, leaving open questions about scalability and expert-conflict resolution as N grows.

Despite explicitly distinguishing the proposed method from concurrent works (Skreta et al. 2025; He et al. 2025) in the related work section, no direct empirical comparison against these closely related PoE/SMC-based diffusion composition methods is provided.

The conditional-expert approximation (Eq. 6/9) and the discriminative-expert endpoint approximation (Eq. 8) are heuristic simplifications without theoretical guarantees on sampling correctness or convergence, and their sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., weight w, number of MCMC/conditional steps) is not thoroughly analyzed.

Reported compute overhead is substantial (e.g., ~30 min per sample for autoregressive video composition), and while acknowledged as a limitation, the paper provides limited discussion of how this scales with more experts or higher resolutions/longer videos.

strengths: Presents a unifying probabilistic (Product-of-Experts) framework that can, in principle, combine heterogeneous sources of knowledge—generative diffusion/flow models, autoregressive models, discriminative VLM rewards, and physics-simulator signals—for controllable visual generation without retraining.

Demonstrates the framework on three distinct and practically relevant applications (graphics-engine-guided image object insertion, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, and layout-controlled text-to-image generation), showing some versatility of the approach.
Includes ablations on conditional sampling (Eq. 6) and SMC resampling/particle count that shed light on which components of the pipeline matter.
Uses a reasonably broad set of automatic metrics (controllability, image/video quality, text/semantic alignment) and includes qualitative figures alongside quantitative tables.
Provides fairly extensive implementation details and appendix material (compute cost, framework instantiations for flow and autoregressive experts) that aid reproducibility to some extent.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is limited: AIS + SMC for compositional sampling has been explored in closely related prior/contemporaneous work (Du et al. 2020/2023, Skreta et al. 2025, He et al. 2025); the paper's main claimed distinguishing feature (per-timestep MCMC kernels vs path-wise importance weights) is asserted rather than rigorously proven—no formal analysis of bias, invariance guarantees under the practical approximations used, or convergence behavior is given.

The 'conditional sampling' mechanism (Eq. 6), which is empirically shown to be important, rests on a heuristic Gaussian approximation with a strong conditional-independence assumption (Eq. 9) and an ad hoc learning-rate hyperparameter w; its validity outside the tested scenarios is unclear.
Evaluation datasets are very small across all three tasks (30, 80, 12, 9, and 50 scenes respectively), limiting statistical confidence in the reported numbers despite reported standard deviations.

Baselines for physics-instructed video generation (Section 4.2) are largely 'same-backbone monolithic' variants (Depth2V/Image2V/Traj2V) rather than dedicated physics-video methods discussed in the related work (e.g., MotionCraft, PhysMotion, Go-with-the-Flow), making the comparison less convincing for that application.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o as an automatic judge for controllability/quality/alignment scores introduces known biases and noise, especially given the small sample sizes; no human evaluation is reported to validate these automatic scores.

Computational overhead is substantial and scales poorly with quality: e.g., Table 4 shows 25x wall-clock increase (L=1 to L=32) for meaningful but incremental mIoU/VQAScore gains, raising questions about practicality relative to end-to-end or lighter-weight alternatives.

The framework requires careful, largely manual per-task configuration of experts, annealing schedules, regional weighting masks, and hyperparameters (T, L, K, w), which undercuts the claim of a general, plug-and-play composition framework and may hinder reproducibility/generalization to new tasks.

Some quantitative results are mixed rather than uniformly favorable (e.g., aesthetic scores in Table 1/2 where baselines sometimes outperform the proposed method), and the paper does not thoroughly discuss or analyze these cases.
Limited exploration of failure modes when expert opinions are incompatible, despite this being explicitly noted as a limitation; no empirical study of robustness to conflicting experts is provided.
